Right: the 2-crust keeps every node with coreness 2 or less, so E, F, G, H and the edges among them are in the accent color, and only the 3-core A to D is dashed." width="100%"} The k-crust contains all nodes with coreness <= `k`. This is the complement of nodes with high coreness values. Put differently, the k-crust is what remains after deleting the `(k+1)`-core: the union of the shells `0` through `k`, i.e., the network's periphery. It is the counterpart of `k_core()`, and is useful for: - studying the periphery of a network separately from its dense core - checking how the outer layers are organized once the core is removed (for example, whether they fall apart into many small pieces) - removing a dominant core before looking for smaller communities The returned graph contains only the crust's nodes and the edges between them; edges into the removed core are dropped. To get every node's coreness at once, use `coreness()`; see also `k_shell()` for a single layer. Degrees count edges without weights. For directed graphs, degree means out-degree. The original graph is not modified. The returned graph keeps the node and edge IDs, labels, weights and attributes of the original. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum coreness value to include. Must be a non-negative integer. `k=0` keeps only isolated nodes, and any `k` at or above the graph's maximum coreness keeps the whole graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New graph containing only the k-crust nodes and their connecting edges. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~k_core`) : The nodes with coreness at least `k`, the opposite of the crust. [](`~k_shell`) : The nodes with coreness exactly `k`. [](`~coreness`) : The coreness of every node. ## Examples {.doc-examples} This graph has a dense cluster `A`-`D` (coreness 3), a loop through `E`, `F` and `G` (coreness 2), and a pendant node `H` (coreness 1). The 2-crust removes the cluster and keeps the rest, with only the edges among them: ::: {#949afb85 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F"), ("F", "G"), ("G", "D"), ("G", "H")] ) crust = graph.k_crust(2) crust.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['E--F', 'F--G', 'G--H'] ``` ::: ::: Raising `k` to the highest coreness gives back every node and edge: ::: {#204d426c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.k_crust(3).count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 12 ``` ::: ::: ### The novel without its center `les_miserables()` links two characters of Victor Hugo's novel when they appear in the same chapter. Taking out the 20 characters with coreness 8 or 9, Valjean and Marius among them, leaves a 7-crust of 57 characters that falls into 15 pieces. Bishop Myriel's circle of ten, from the start of the novel, is one of them: ::: {#d7c92e3c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} novel = ec.les_miserables() crust = novel.k_crust(7) pieces = sorted(crust.weakly_connected_components(), key=len) crust.count_nodes(), len(pieces), [len(p) for p in pieces[-3:]] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (57, 15, [3, 10, 30]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#4bed68b1 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} myriel = crust.node_connected_component("Myriel") crust.plot(highlight=list(myriel), label_by="label", seed=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
